clue.text: "The old President gets but one daily" — how rumours get around!

parts.note: George Bush senior, US President 1989-93, an ex-President by the time of this puzzle
the Daily Telegraph is one of Britain's daily newspapers

explanation.surface: A quoted complaint that a former president reads only a single newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks hide the joke: the line reads like a gripe about George Bush's reading habits. The Telegraph is a British daily paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The bush telegraph is the informal word-of-mouth network by which gossip spreads quickly.

clue.text: Reaction on getting wind of cup size on topless movie star

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece placed on another sits above it

parts.note: B is a bra cup size

indicators.note: a word that goes topless loses its top, here its first letter

parts.note: Raquel Welch, the film actress

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of someone reacting to a glimpse of a busty film star.
explanation.walkthrough: Raquel Welch was a 1960s film star famous for her figure; 'topless' drops her first letter to leave ELCH, and 'on' sets the cup size B on top of it in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A belch is the body's reaction to trapped wind, the gas coming up and out.

clue.text: Nut-case foreign court into S and M

indicators.note: the reworked letters go into the gap between the S and the M

parts.note: the letter S as written
the letter M as written

indicators.note: something made foreign is turned strange, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A foreign judge with an S and M habit sounds like a tabloid scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut-case' looks like an insult for a madman; read literally it is the case that holds the nuts, slang for testicles. 'Foreign' rearranges COURT to CROTU, which goes 'into' S and M.
explanation.definitionFit: The scrotum is the pouch of skin holding the testicles, which slang calls nuts.

clue.text: Play with oneself, being shy?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: British slang for masturbating
second meaning: to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shy' wants to be the adjective timid; here it is the verb meaning throw. To toss off is British slang for masturbating.
explanation.definitionFit: The one word covers both crude slang for self-pleasuring and an ordinary verb for throwing something.

clue.text: Garland on fast in spare time

indicators.note: in a down clue the garland sits on top of the next piece

parts.note: a lei is a Hawaiian garland of flowers
fast in the sense of firmly fixed, as in holding fast, means sure

explanation.surface: Someone spends their days off weaving garlands while fasting.
explanation.definitionFit: Leisure is free time, the hours left over after work and duties.

clue.text: Light-headed trespasser, grand old Italian, gets engaged

parts.note: G is slang for a grand, a thousand pounds
taken as written
I is the abbreviation for Italian, as on international car plates
a mechanism locks when its parts engage and hold fast

explanation.surface: A dizzy intruder and an old Italian grandee announce their engagement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Light-headed' looks like dizzy; it means fair-haired. Goldilocks walked into the three bears' house uninvited.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldilocks of the fairy tale has golden hair and trespasses in the bears' cottage.

clue.text: Not what a retainer suffers from?

definitions.text: Not what a retainer suffers from?

parts.words: Not what a retainer suffers from?
parts.note: a retainer is read as one who retains, and a person who keeps their memories is free of forgetting

explanation.walkthrough: A retainer usually means an old family servant or a dental brace; here it is literally someone who retains things, such as memories.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is loss of memory, the opposite of retaining what one has learned.

clue.text: Hague's first (hey, hey!) to secure vote of the masses

indicators.note: first picks out the opening letter of the Tory leader's name

parts.note: William Hague, Conservative leader at the time

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it, so the two cries hold the vote between them

parts.note: oi is a British shout to get attention, like hey, so two of them
a poll is a vote

explanation.surface: William Hague, cheered on with shouts, tries to win the popular vote.
explanation.walkthrough: Oi is the rough British equivalent of hey, so the doubled shout gives two OIs, which 'to secure' wraps round POLL to make OIPOLLOI; 'first' gives H from Hague to go in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoi polloi is a Greek phrase for the common people, the ordinary crowd.

clue.text: Warning signals — that they're coming back?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bright rockets fired to signal distress or danger
second meaning: flared trousers, the wide-bottomed 1970s fashion, keep returning to style

explanation.walkthrough: The second half reads like part of the warning; it is a joke about fashion, since flared trousers come back into style every so often.
explanation.definitionFit: Distress rockets and wide-legged trousers share the one name, and the trousers are famous for their revivals.

clue.text: State of Dicky: the man's lost his head entertaining Number One

parts.note: dicky is British slang for unwell or shaky, as in a dicky heart

indicators.note: to entertain a guest is to have them inside, so the shortened word holds the next piece
losing a head means the word drops its first letter

parts.note: his means the man's
No. I, number one written with NO and the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Someone frets about the state of a man called Dicky who has lost his head while entertaining.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dicky' looks like a name; it is the British word for poorly. 'Lost his head' takes the first letter from HIS to leave IS, and 'entertaining' puts NO and I inside it, giving INOIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Illinois is one of the fifty states of the USA, home of Chicago.

clue.text: Birds getting intercourse (sex)

parts.note: chat is talk, the social sense of intercourse
S is the abbreviation for sex, as on old forms (M or F)

explanation.surface: Women (birds, in British slang) are getting some sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Birds' looks like the British slang for women and 'intercourse' looks sexual; the birds are real birds and the intercourse is conversation.
explanation.definitionFit: Chats are small songbirds such as the stonechat and the whinchat.

clue.text: Archer's got front — and lip

parts.note: Cupid is the archer god of love, so this means Cupid's
the bow is the front of a ship

explanation.surface: Jeffrey Archer is accused of having a cheek and some lip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Archer' suggests the novelist Jeffrey Archer and 'front' and 'lip' suggest cheek; the archer is Cupid, the front is a ship's bow.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cupid's bow is the double curve of the upper lip, shaped like the god's bow.

clue.text: Degenerate, fashionably nostalgic Michael …

parts.note: retro describes styles that fashionably revive the past
Michael Grade, the British TV executive who ran Channel 4

explanation.surface: A dig at a TV boss, Michael, for being decadent and stuck in the past.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Grade was a well-known British television executive, accused of pushing sleaze on Channel 4.
explanation.definitionFit: Retrograde as an adjective means going backwards or getting worse, as a decline does.

clue.text: Be the first to show Hague's finally following Blair?

indicators.note: the letter from Hague comes after Blair's title

parts.note: Tony Blair was the British premier, the prime minister

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of the word

parts.note: William Hague, Conservative leader, whose name ends in E

explanation.surface: Will Hague finally be the first to show, ahead of Tony Blair?
explanation.walkthrough: Blair simply gives his job title, premier. 'Finally' takes the last letter of Hague, and 'following' puts it after PREMIER.
explanation.definitionFit: To premiere a film or play is to give its first public showing.

clue.text: … to manage half of Blair's offspring degenerate

parts.note: to run a business is to manage it

indicators.note: half of means only the first two of the four letters are kept

parts.note: Tony is Blair's first name
seed is an old word for offspring, as in the seed of Abraham

explanation.surface: It continues from 12-down, joking about running half of Tony Blair's degenerate children.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses link this to 12-down, but each clue stands alone. 'Half of' Blair's first name TONY gives TO.
explanation.definitionFit: To run to seed is an idiom for going to pot, like a vegetable that bolts and goes useless.

clue.text: Mystic Meg's rude craft: going topless

definitions.note: the 's stands for is: Mystic Meg is an oracle

indicators.note: going topless means losing the top, the first letter

parts.note: a coracle is a small primitive boat, rude meaning crude or roughly made

explanation.surface: The tabloid astrologer Mystic Meg's crude craft turns out to be stripping off.
explanation.walkthrough: Mystic Meg was the astrologer of the Sun newspaper and the National Lottery show. 'Rude' means primitive here, and 'going topless' takes the first letter off CORACLE.
explanation.definitionFit: An oracle is a prophet who foretells the future, as a tabloid fortune-teller claims to.

clue.text: Would-be hooker's view on Right

definitions.note: the 's is read as is: an angler is someone who hopes to hook a fish

indicators.note: the view comes on, that is before, the abbreviation in an across answer

parts.note: an angle is a point of view

explanation.surface: An aspiring prostitute's opinions turn out to be right-wing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooker' suggests a prostitute; the hooking is of fish. 'On' puts the view ANGLE before R for Right.
explanation.definitionFit: An angler fishes with rod and line, trying to hook a catch.

clue.text: Nautical mishap — one's lost nuts

indicators.note: a mishap throws things into disorder, so the letters are rearranged
lost tells us the letter for one goes missing from the jumble

parts.note: A means one, as in a pound

explanation.surface: After a nautical mishap someone has lost the nuts and bolts.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a composite anagram: 'mishap' jumbles NAUTICAL and 'lost' says one A goes missing from it, so the remaining seven letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunatic as an adjective means crazy, the same sense as the slang word for mad.

clue.text: What our Brian would be: able to go round fooling one's sexual partner?

indicators.note: to go round something is to surround it, so the word for able encloses the other piece

parts.note: fit means able, as in fit to work
the setter casts Brian as a would-be monarch, so he would be a king, as Brian of Life of Brian is hailed as a messiah king

explanation.surface: A man's sexual deceptions are blamed on someone called Brian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To go round' puts FIT around A KING. The phrase is used of pretending to have an orgasm.
explanation.definitionFit: Faking it means pretending pleasure in bed, a way of deceiving a lover about satisfaction.

clue.text: Intimate second TV series

parts.note: an intimate is a close friend

explanation.surface: An intimate second series of a television programme.
explanation.definitionFit: Friends was the hugely popular American sitcom about six New Yorkers.

clue.text: Opera makes Castro-type rise up firm

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising up means reading from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Fidel Castro is Cuban, so a Castro-type is a Cuban
CO is the abbreviation for company, a firm

explanation.surface: A rousing opera inspires a Castro-style uprising against a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rise up' fits the surface of a revolution, but in a down clue it is the reversal signal: the Cuban leader's nationality read from the bottom gives NABUC.
explanation.definitionFit: Nabucco is Verdi's opera about Nebuchadnezzar, with the famous chorus of the Hebrew slaves.

clue.text: The product of de-capitalised New Labour?

definitions.text: The product of de-capitalised New Labour?

parts.words: The product of de-capitalised New Labour?
parts.note: with its capitals removed the party name becomes a fresh delivery of a baby, whose product is a person delivered a second time

explanation.walkthrough: Taking the capitals off New Labour, the party, gives new labour, a fresh childbirth; what it delivers has been through birth again. It also mocks evangelical zeal for Blair's rebranded party.
explanation.definitionFit: Born-again describes someone converted to fervent faith, as if given a second birth.

clue.text: Corporately prominent, honoured types taking ecstasy

definitions.note: corporately is read as bodily, from corpus: a prominent body is a big one

indicators.note: taking means the honoured types take the drug along with them, so it is added on

parts.note: OBEs are people honoured with the Order of the British Empire
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Honours-list business leaders are caught taking ecstasy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corporately' points at companies; it means bodily. An OBE is a British honour, and 'taking' adds E for ecstasy after OBES.
explanation.definitionFit: Obese means very fat, so the body stands out prominently.

clue.text: Rolls up, oily and unctuous

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: a boat that keels rolls over onto its side

explanation.surface: A smarmy man in a Rolls-Royce rolls up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rolls up' looks like arriving; it is a verb for tipping over, then turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleek can describe someone smooth and slick in manner, a smarmy flatterer.

clue.text: Flipping Forte admirer's crap

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters are read backwards

parts.note: F is the musical abbreviation for forte, loud
a fan is an admirer

explanation.surface: An exasperated fan dismisses the Forte hotel chain as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' reads as a mild British swearword; it is the reversal signal. Naff is British slang for tacky or rubbish.
explanation.definitionFit: Naff is British slang for something cheap, tasteless or rubbish.

clue.text: Practice bondage and relax before shower

indicators.note: relax comes before shower in the answer

parts.note: to rest is to relax
rain falls in showers

explanation.surface: A kinky routine: tie someone up, then unwind before a shower.
explanation.definitionFit: To restrain someone is to hold them bound, which is what bondage involves.

clue.text: Topless demonstrator? Liar!

indicators.note: topless means losing the top letter

parts.note: a marcher is a demonstrator on a protest march

explanation.surface: A topless protester is shouted down as a liar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' takes the first letter off MARCHER. Jeffrey Archer, the Tory novelist, was exposed in 1999 for lying in a libel case and later jailed for perjury.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eye calls Lord Archer a liar after his perjury scandal, a topical example of one.

clue.text: OK, hussy forced out but is she really entitled to be called this?

definitions.text: is she really entitled to be called this?

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A brazen woman is forced out, but does she deserve her title?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forced' sits beside 'out' as if the hussy is expelled; it is part of the letters to rearrange. Sarah Ferguson kept her title after divorcing Prince Andrew.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarah Ferguson still used the royal title after her 1996 divorce, which many felt she no longer deserved.
